questions.title: Debugging a WHERE = NULL mistake
questions.prompt: A junior developer writes WHERE MiddleName = NULL to find customers with no middle name recorded, and gets zero rows back — even though many customers genuinely have a NULL MiddleName. What's actually wrong with that query, and how should they fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: NULL represents an unknown or not-applicable value, not zero or an empty string. Because it's unknown, NULL can't be said to equal anything — not even another NULL — so any comparison using the = operator against NULL evaluates to unknown (treated as false), never true. That means WHERE MiddleName = NULL will always return zero rows, regardless of how many rows actually have a NULL MiddleName, because the comparison can never succeed. The fix is to use the special IS NULL syntax instead: WHERE MiddleName IS NULL. IS NULL isn't a comparison operator — it's dedicated syntax built specifically to test for the absence of a value, and it works correctly where = cannot. The same logic applies to IS NOT NULL for the opposite case.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd point out is that this isn't a typo or syntax error — the query runs fine, it just silently returns the wrong answer, which is the dangerous kind of bug. I'd explain that NULL means 'unknown,' and you can't compare an unknown value to anything using = and expect a meaningful true or false — SQL Server treats that comparison as unknown, which gets filtered out just like false. So WHERE MiddleName = NULL isn't matching NULLs, it's failing to match anything at all. The fix is WHERE MiddleName IS NULL, which is purpose-built syntax for exactly this case rather than a regular comparison. If the goal were actually to display something readable instead of filtering, I'd reach for ISNULL(MiddleName, '(none)') or COALESCE for more than two fallback values.
commonMistakes: Not realizing the query runs without error and silently returns the wrong result, rather than throwing an obvious failure
Treating NULL as if it were an empty string or zero instead of 'unknown'
Using = NULL or <> NULL anywhere instead of IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
Confusing ISNULL() (replaces a NULL with a default, two arguments) with IS NULL (tests for NULL)
keyPoints: NULL means unknown/not applicable, not zero or empty string
= NULL always evaluates to unknown/false, never true
IS NULL / IS NOT NULL is the only correct way to test for NULL
ISNULL()/COALESCE() substitute a default value rather than test for NULL

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses why = NULL fails silently
Provides the correct fix (IS NULL)
Mentions ISNULL/COALESCE as a related but different tool

questions.title: Diagnosing an accidental Cartesian product
questions.prompt: A query joining a 500-row Products table to a 100,000-row OrderDetail table unexpectedly returns 50 million rows instead of something in the few-hundred-thousand range. What almost certainly went wrong, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: 50 million is exactly 500 times 100,000 -- the row-count signature of a Cartesian product, where every row of one table gets paired with every row of the other instead of only matching rows being paired. The most common real-world cause isn't a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- it's a missing or ineffective ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join: either the ON clause is left out entirely (old-style comma join with no join condition), or it exists but evaluates to true for nearly every row combination (for example ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which doesn't actually relate the two tables). To confirm it, check the join's ON clause first for a missing or non-relating condition, and as a general habit, sanity-check the row count after any join: if two tables of roughly 500 and 100,000 rows produce millions of result rows instead of a number in that rough range, that's an immediate signal to re-check the ON clause rather than assume the data is simply that large.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd notice is that 50 million is suspiciously close to 500 times 100,000 -- that's the fingerprint of a Cartesian product, not a coincidence. My first move is to go straight to the ON clause of the join and check two things: is it missing entirely, which happens with old comma-style joins that have no join condition at all, or does it exist but not actually relate the two tables -- something like ON p.Name IS NOT NULL, which is true for almost every row and produces a Cartesian product in disguise even though there's technically an ON clause sitting there. Once I fix the condition to something that actually ties the tables together, like p.ProductID = sod.ProductID, I'd re-run the query and expect the row count to land in the same rough range as the bigger of the two tables, not multiply them together. I've made this a habit on every join I write now: sanity-check the row count before trusting the result.
questions.example:
-- BUG: no join condition at all -- a Cartesian product
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p, Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod;

-- BUG: ON clause exists but doesn't relate the tables
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.Name IS NOT NULL;

-- FIXED: a real join condition tying the tables together
SELECT p.Name, sod.OrderQty
FROM Production.Product AS p
INNER JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail AS sod
    ON p.ProductID = sod.ProductID;
commonMistakes: Assuming the data itself is just 'that big' instead of suspecting the join condition first
Not recognizing that an ON clause can exist and still produce a Cartesian product if it doesn't genuinely relate the tables
Never sanity-checking row counts after writing a join, so the problem isn't caught until it hits production
Confusing this with a deliberate CROSS JOIN -- the accidental version almost always comes from a broken or missing ON condition on what was meant to be a normal join
keyPoints: Row count multiplying (500 x 100,000) instead of adding is the signature of a Cartesian product
Most accidental Cartesian products come from a missing or non-relating ON clause
Old-style comma joins with no ON clause default to a Cartesian product
An ON clause that's technically present but true for nearly every row is just as dangerous as none at all
Sanity-check row counts after any join as a standing habit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the Cartesian product and the row-count math
Correctly identifies missing/ineffective ON clause as the cause
Describes a practical way to catch this before production

questions.title: SUM inflated after joining a one-to-many table
questions.prompt: A query joins SalesOrderHeader to SalesOrderDetail and correctly totals each order with SUM(LineTotal). After adding a third join to a Promotion table -- where some orders have more than one matching promotion row -- the total for those specific orders suddenly doubles or triples, even though nothing about the actual sales changed. The join conditions are all correct and genuinely relate the tables. What's going on, and how would you fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: This isn't a Cartesian product -- every join condition is correct and genuinely relates the tables -- it's join fan-out, which happens whenever a correct join still has a one-to-many relationship on one side. Each SalesOrderDetail row that matches more than one Promotion row gets physically duplicated once per matching promotion before SUM ever runs, so SUM(LineTotal) is now adding the same line total two or three times for any order whose promotion happens to match more than once, while orders with exactly one (or zero) matching promotions are unaffected. The fix is to never combine two separate one-to-many expansions in a single flat join and then aggregate at the end -- instead, pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the grain actually needed, in its own subquery or CTE, before joining. Here, that means computing the order total from SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail alone first, and only joining Promotion afterward (or in a separate query) if promotion details are genuinely needed, rather than letting its fan-out multiply rows that feed directly into the order-total SUM.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out first that this isn't the Cartesian-product bug people usually learn about -- every join condition here is correct and really does relate the tables. This is fan-out: joining in a table that can legitimately match more than one row per order duplicates the order-detail rows underneath it, once per matching promotion, before the SUM even runs. So an order with two matching promotions gets its LineTotal counted twice, not because the math is wrong, but because the row genuinely got duplicated first. My fix is to separate the two aggregations: compute each order's total from just SalesOrderHeader and SalesOrderDetail in a CTE first, completely isolated from the Promotion join, and only bring Promotion into a separate query (or join it after the order total is already locked in) if I actually need promotion-level detail. The rule I'd apply going forward is never to let two independent one-to-many joins sit in the same flat query feeding one aggregate -- pre-aggregate each one to the grain I need first.
questions.example:
-- WRONG: Promotion's fan-out inflates the order total
SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
JOIN Sales.SpecialOfferProduct promo ON promo.ProductID = sod.ProductID
GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID;

-- FIXED: order total computed in isolation, before any promotion join
WITH OrderTotals AS (
    SELECT soh.SalesOrderID, SUM(sod.LineTotal) AS OrderTotal
    FROM Sales.SalesOrderHeader soh
    JOIN Sales.SalesOrderDetail sod ON sod.SalesOrderID = soh.SalesOrderID
    GROUP BY soh.SalesOrderID
)
SELECT * FROM OrderTotals;
commonMistakes: Assuming a correct, relating join condition rules out row duplication entirely
Not comparing row counts (or a known-good total) before and after adding the third join
Reaching for SUM(DISTINCT ...) as a quick fix, which only coincidentally works and breaks again as soon as two genuinely different line totals happen to match
Combining two separate one-to-many expansions in one flat query feeding a single aggregate, instead of pre-aggregating each one to the grain actually needed
keyPoints: A correct join condition can still fan out rows when the relationship is genuinely one-to-many
Fan-out duplicates rows before aggregation runs, inflating any SUM downstream
This is distinct from a Cartesian product, which comes from a missing or non-relating join condition
Fix: pre-aggregate each one-to-many relationship to the needed grain in its own subquery/CTE before joining further

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses join fan-out (not a Cartesian product)
Explains why the duplication inflates the SUM
Proposes a correct fix (pre-aggregating before joining further)

questions.title: A Delta write fails with a schema mismatch error
questions.prompt: You run a daily append job writing a DataFrame into an existing Delta table, and it suddenly fails with a schema mismatch error after the source added a new column. What's happening, and what are your two realistic options to fix it?
questions.modelAnswer: Delta enforces schema by default: an append whose DataFrame schema doesn't exactly match the target table's schema is rejected rather than silently written, which is schema enforcement protecting the table from accidental corruption. There are two realistic options. First, if the new column is actually wanted in the table going forward, intentionally allow it in with schema evolution — adding .option('mergeSchema', 'true') on the write (or enabling spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled) adds the new column to the table's schema, backfilling NULL for every row written before that column existed. Second, if the new column wasn't actually wanted in this table yet, select only the originally expected columns out of the DataFrame before writing, keeping the table's schema stable and letting the write succeed unchanged. Which option is right depends entirely on whether the new column should actually become part of the table now.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd first confirm this is schema enforcement doing its job, not a bug -- Delta deliberately rejects a write whose schema doesn't match rather than silently writing a half-matching row. Then it comes down to one question: do I actually want this new column in the table right now? If yes, I'd add mergeSchema as true on the write, which performs schema evolution -- it adds the column going forward and backfills NULL for every historical row, which I'd want the team to know about so nobody's surprised by NULLs appearing in older data. If the column isn't ready to be part of this table yet, I'd just select the DataFrame down to the columns the table already expects before writing, which keeps the schema stable and lets the job succeed without silently picking up something nobody's reviewed.
questions.example:
# Option 1: intentionally evolve the schema
raw_df.write.format("delta").mode("append").option("mergeSchema", "true").saveAsTable("sales_bronze")

# Option 2: keep the existing schema, drop the new column for now
raw_df.select("OrderId", "Amount", "OrderDate").write.format("delta").mode("append").saveAsTable("sales_bronze")
commonMistakes: Assuming a schema mismatch error is a bug in Delta rather than deliberate schema enforcement
Turning on mergeSchema everywhere as a default habit instead of deciding deliberately whether the new column belongs in the table
Not realizing older rows get backfilled with NULL for a newly added column after schema evolution
Trying to force the write through without addressing the schema difference at all, rather than choosing one of the two real options
keyPoints: Schema enforcement blocks a mismatched write by default to protect the table
mergeSchema enables intentional schema evolution, adding the new column going forward
The alternative is trimming the DataFrame back to the existing schema before writing
Schema evolution backfills NULL for historical rows under the newly added column

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses schema enforcement as the cause
Describes the mergeSchema/schema evolution option
Describes the alternative of trimming the DataFrame to the existing schema

questions.title: Terraform apply fails saying a resource already exists
questions.prompt: You run terraform apply to provision a storage account that a teammate already created manually in the Azure portal, and it fails saying the resource already exists. Terraform's configuration is correct. What's the real problem, and how do you fix it without just deleting the existing resource?
questions.modelAnswer: Terraform's state file is its own record of what it believes it manages; a resource that exists in Azure but was never created through Terraform isn't in that state file, so Terraform has no way to know it already exists and tries to create a duplicate, which Azure rejects since the name must be unique. The fix (without deleting anything) is terraform import, which tells Terraform 'this resource already exists at this address, start tracking it in state without creating it' -- after import, a subsequent plan should show no changes if the configuration matches the real resource's settings exactly, or a diff if they don't match, which then needs reconciling.
questions.professionalAnswer: The real issue isn't the configuration — it's that Terraform's state file has no idea this resource exists, because it was created by hand instead of through Terraform. Terraform only ever knows about what's recorded in its own state, not everything that's actually sitting in the subscription, so it tries to create a new one and Azure rejects it as a duplicate name. Rather than deleting the manually-created resource and losing whatever's already configured on it, I'd run terraform import to attach that existing resource to the matching address in my configuration, which starts tracking it in state without touching it. After that, I'd run plan again — if my configuration doesn't exactly match the real resource's settings, plan will show a diff I still need to reconcile, so import isn't quite the end of the story by itself.
commonMistakes: Deleting the manually-created resource just to let Terraform create a fresh one, losing any data/config already on it
Not realizing Terraform's state file, not the configuration, is what tracks what Terraform believes exists
Forgetting that after import, the configuration still needs to match the real resource's actual settings or the next plan will show an unwanted diff
Assuming the 'already exists' error means the configuration itself is wrong, rather than a state-tracking gap
keyPoints: Terraform only knows about what's in its state file, not everything that exists in the cloud
terraform import links an existing resource to a config address without recreating it
Verify with plan afterward that the configuration matches reality
Deleting a manually-created resource to avoid this is risky and unnecessary

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the state-file gap as the cause
Proposes terraform import as the fix
Notes the need to verify configuration matches after import

questions.title: Queries against a Delta table have gotten slow due to too many small files
questions.prompt: A Delta table that receives frequent small append writes throughout the day has gradually gotten much slower to query, even though the total amount of data hasn't grown dramatically. What's the likely cause, and what command addresses it?
questions.modelAnswer: Frequent small appends each write their own small Parquet file underneath the Delta table, and over time this produces the 'small file problem' -- instead of a reasonable number of appropriately-sized files, the table ends up backed by thousands of tiny ones. Reading the table means opening and reading from every one of those files, and the per-file overhead (opening, reading metadata/footer, closing) starts to dominate query time even though the actual data volume is the same. The fix is running OPTIMIZE on the table, which compacts many small files into a smaller number of appropriately-sized ones (optionally combined with ZORDER BY on a frequently-filtered column to colocate related data within those files), directly addressing the file-count problem without changing the data itself.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first instinct wouldn't be to throw more compute at this — it's worth checking file count and size before assuming the cluster needs to be bigger. Frequent small appends are a classic way to end up with the small file problem: every little write creates its own small Parquet file, and eventually the table is backed by far more files than it needs, so just opening and closing each one starts to dominate query time even though the data itself hasn't grown much. Running OPTIMIZE on the table compacts those small files into a sensible number of larger ones, and if there's a column that's frequently filtered on, I'd pair it with ZORDER BY that column to colocate related data within the compacted files too. I'd also make sure I'm not confusing this with VACUUM, which removes old unreferenced files rather than compacting current ones — they solve two different problems.
commonMistakes: Assuming slow queries always mean more compute/cluster size is needed, rather than checking file count/size first
Not running OPTIMIZE periodically on tables with frequent small writes
Confusing OPTIMIZE (compacts files) with VACUUM (removes old, unreferenced files) -- they solve different problems
Running OPTIMIZE once and assuming the small-file problem is permanently solved, rather than scheduling it to run periodically
keyPoints: Frequent small appends create many small underlying files (the small file problem)
Per-file overhead dominates query time once file count grows large
OPTIMIZE compacts small files into larger ones
ZORDER can be combined with OPTIMIZE for frequently-filtered columns

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the small-file problem
Proposes OPTIMIZE as the fix
Distinguishes OPTIMIZE from VACUUM

questions.title: Access Denied on S3 despite a seemingly correct IAM policy
questions.prompt: An application role has an IAM policy that explicitly allows s3:GetObject on a bucket, but every request still returns Access Denied. The bucket policy doesn't mention this role at all. What's the most likely explanation, and how would you confirm it?
questions.modelAnswer: An explicit Deny anywhere in the evaluation -- an IAM policy, a bucket policy, an Organizations SCP, or S3 Block Public Access in some cases -- always overrides an Allow, no matter where that Allow comes from. Since the role's own IAM policy allows the action but requests still fail, the most likely explanation is a Deny sitting somewhere else entirely: a common real cause is a bucket policy with a condition-based Deny, such as denying any request where aws:SecureTransport is false (enforcing HTTPS), or denying access outside a specific VPC endpoint -- neither of which needs to mention the role by name to still block it. To confirm, check the bucket policy itself for any Deny statement and its conditions, check for an applicable Organizations SCP if the account is part of an organization, and use the IAM policy simulator (or IAM Access Analyzer) to evaluate what the actual effective permission is for that specific request, since simulating the request directly is far more reliable than manually reasoning through every policy that could apply.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first thing I'd remind myself is that Deny always wins, from anywhere, so I wouldn't stop at the IAM policy just because it looks right. I'd go check the bucket policy next, specifically looking for a condition-based Deny -- something like denying any request where SecureTransport is false, which is a very common pattern for enforcing HTTPS and wouldn't need to name this role at all to still block it. If the account is part of an AWS Organization, I'd also check for an SCP that might be denying the action account-wide. Rather than trying to manually trace through every policy that could apply, I'd just run the request through the IAM policy simulator, which tells me directly what the effective permission actually is and, usually, exactly which policy is the one doing the denying.
commonMistakes: Only checking the IAM policy that was already confirmed allows the action, without checking the bucket policy or SCPs for an explicit Deny
Not knowing an explicit Deny anywhere in the evaluation always overrides an Allow, regardless of which policy it's in
Manually reasoning through every policy instead of using the IAM policy simulator or Access Analyzer to get the actual effective permission
Overlooking S3 Block Public Access settings as another place a Deny-like block can originate
keyPoints: An explicit Deny anywhere (IAM policy, bucket policy, SCP) always overrides an Allow
A condition-based Deny (e.g., enforcing HTTPS via aws:SecureTransport) doesn't need to name the role to block it
Check the bucket policy and any applicable SCPs, not just the role's own IAM policy
The IAM policy simulator / Access Analyzer gives the actual effective permission directly

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains that Deny overrides Allow regardless of source
Identifies a realistic Deny source (bucket policy condition, SCP)
Describes a concrete way to confirm it (simulator/Access Analyzer)

questions.title: Athena returns zero rows for data that's definitely in S3
questions.prompt: You confirm new Parquet files landed in s3://data-lake/sales/year=2026/month=10/ an hour ago, but SELECT * FROM sales WHERE year=2026 AND month=10 in Athena returns zero rows. What's the most likely cause, and what command fixes it?
questions.modelAnswer: Athena doesn't automatically know about a new partition folder just because files landed at the right S3 path -- for a Hive-style partitioned table, Athena (through the Glue Data Catalog) only queries partitions that have actually been registered in the catalog's partition metadata, and a brand-new partition folder isn't registered there until something explicitly adds it. The fix is running MSCK REPAIR TABLE sales, which scans the table's S3 location and registers any partitions it finds that aren't yet in the catalog, or using ALTER TABLE sales ADD PARTITION to add just the one new partition directly, which is typically faster when only a single new partition needs registering. To confirm this is actually the cause before running either command, SHOW PARTITIONS sales will show whether year=2026/month=10 is currently listed as a registered partition at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: My first move, before running any fix, is SHOW PARTITIONS sales, just to confirm this is actually a missing-partition problem and not something else entirely. If year=2026/month=10 isn't listed, that confirms it -- Athena genuinely has no idea that partition exists yet, even though the files are sitting right there in S3. For a single new partition like this, I'd usually reach for ALTER TABLE sales ADD PARTITION (year=2026, month=10) LOCATION '...' rather than MSCK REPAIR TABLE, since repair scans the entire table's S3 location to find every missing partition, which can get slow on a table that already has a lot of partitions -- ADD PARTITION targets exactly the one I already know is missing.
commonMistakes: Assuming Athena automatically discovers new partition folders the moment files land in S3
Not running SHOW PARTITIONS first to confirm the partition is actually missing from the catalog
Always reaching for MSCK REPAIR TABLE on a large table instead of ADD PARTITION for a single known new partition
Treating the zero rows as a permissions issue instead of a catalog-registration issue
keyPoints: New S3 partition folders aren't visible to Athena until registered in the Glue Catalog
MSCK REPAIR TABLE scans the whole table location and registers any missing Hive-style partitions
ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION registers one partition directly and is often faster for a single new one
SHOW PARTITIONS confirms what's currently registered before you act

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the missing-partition-registration cause
Gives the correct fix command(s)
Describes a concrete way to confirm the diagnosis first

questions.title: A Glue job isn't picking up files you expect it to reprocess
questions.prompt: You fix a bug in a Glue ETL job's transformation logic and rerun it, expecting it to reprocess all the source files in S3 with the corrected logic. Instead, it finishes almost instantly and the output doesn't change. What's the most likely cause, and how do you force it to reprocess everything?
questions.modelAnswer: Glue job bookmarks are the most likely cause -- bookmarks track which source data (by file path/timestamp, or a tracked column for JDBC sources) the job has already processed, specifically so a scheduled rerun only picks up new data instead of reprocessing everything each time. Since the source files themselves haven't changed -- only the job's transformation code did -- the bookmark still considers those files already processed and skips them, which is exactly why the job finishes almost instantly with no new output: it has nothing new to do by its own tracking, even though the logic that would process it differently now is sitting right there. To force a full reprocess, reset the job bookmark -- through the Glue console's 'Reset job bookmark' action or the AWS CLI's reset-job-bookmark command -- before the next run, which clears its memory of what's already been processed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd recognize this immediately as a job bookmark issue rather than assume the job itself is broken -- bookmarks are specifically designed to make a rerun skip data it's already seen, and they have no concept of 'the code changed, so re-check everything.' The files haven't changed, so as far as the bookmark is concerned, there's nothing new to process, which explains exactly why it finished instantly with no difference in output. To force it to actually reprocess everything with the fixed logic, I'd reset the bookmark for that specific job before running it again -- aws glue reset-job-bookmark --job-name my-job -- and I'd keep in mind that's scoped to this one job, so if another job reads the same source data, its own bookmark is untouched by this reset.
questions.example: aws glue reset-job-bookmark --job-name my-transform-job
commonMistakes: Assuming the job itself is broken instead of recognizing job bookmarks are intentionally skipping already-seen files
Not realizing a code fix doesn't change what the bookmark considers 'already processed'
Resetting bookmarks as a default habit even when incremental processing is actually what's wanted
Assuming resetting one job's bookmark affects other jobs reading the same source data
keyPoints: Glue job bookmarks track already-processed source data to support incremental runs
A bookmark has no awareness that the job's own logic changed -- it only tracks what data it's already seen
reset-job-bookmark (console or CLI) forces a full reprocess on the next run
Bookmarks are scoped per job, not shared across other jobs reading the same source

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses job bookmarks as the cause
Gives the correct fix (reset-job-bookmark)
Notes bookmarks are per-job scoped

questions.title: A Lambda function starts timing out on larger files
questions.prompt: A Lambda function that processes CSV files dropped into S3 has worked reliably for months, but starts failing with timeout errors after the source system began sending noticeably larger files. What's actually going on, and what are your realistic options?
questions.modelAnswer: Lambda has a hard maximum execution timeout (configurable per function, but capped at 15 minutes) and a configurable memory allocation that also scales the CPU available to the function. A larger file takes proportionally longer to read and process, and once that processing time exceeds the function's configured timeout, Lambda kills the invocation mid-execution regardless of how close it was to finishing -- that's the direct cause of the new failures. The realistic options are: increase the configured timeout and/or memory (more memory also grants more CPU within Lambda's limits, which can meaningfully speed up processing, not just allow more time), which buys headroom for files up to some larger size; or, if file sizes are on an open-ended growth trend rather than a one-time bump, recognize that Lambda is fundamentally built for short, bounded invocations, not arbitrarily large batch processing, and move that specific workload to a service designed for it -- a Glue ETL job, EMR/Spark, or a Fargate task -- rather than continuing to push against Lambda's ceiling.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd start in CloudWatch Logs to see roughly how far the function got before being killed, just to confirm this really is a timeout and not some other new error. Assuming it is, the quick fix is bumping the timeout and memory -- and I'd actually bump memory first, since more memory also means more CPU in Lambda, which can meaningfully cut processing time rather than just buying more clock time to hit the same slow code. But I'd ask the team how these file sizes are expected to trend before stopping there -- if this was a one-time larger batch, tuning the limits is probably fine. If file sizes are only going to keep growing, I wouldn't keep nudging Lambda's limits upward indefinitely; I'd move that processing step to something actually built for larger, longer-running batch work, like a Glue job, since Lambda was never designed to be the tool for open-ended batch sizes in the first place.
commonMistakes: Assuming Lambda's timeout can be raised indefinitely instead of knowing it's hard-capped at 15 minutes
Treating increased memory purely as a time lever, without realizing it also increases available CPU and cost
Treating a timeout purely as a bug to patch instead of an architectural-fit signal
Continuing to tune Lambda's limits for a workload whose file sizes keep growing, instead of migrating to a batch-appropriate service
keyPoints: Lambda has a hard max timeout (15 minutes) and configurable memory that also scales CPU
Larger files increase processing time, eventually exceeding the configured timeout
Quick fix: raise timeout and/or memory within Lambda's limits
Durable fix for open-ended growth: move the workload to Glue, EMR, or Fargate, since Lambda isn't built for unbounded batch processing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly diagnoses the timeout as a size-vs-limit issue
Describes the quick fix (timeout/memory) accurately
Recognizes when to move off Lambda entirely for this workload

questions.title: Why Dev, QA, and Production stay separate
questions.prompt: Why does a BI team typically maintain separate Dev, QA, and Production SQL Server environments, and promote a change through them in that fixed order, instead of just building and testing directly against the Production database that live reports and real users already depend on?
questions.modelAnswer: Dev is where new work is actually built, and it's expected to be unstable -- half-finished packages, broken queries, and throwaway test data are all normal there, and critically, none of that instability is visible to anyone who depends on real numbers. QA is a separate, more stable environment with data that resembles Production, used specifically to verify a change behaves correctly before any real user is ever exposed to it -- this is where testing is supposed to happen, not in Dev and not in Production. Production is the environment real business users and live reports actually run against, and it's deliberately the last environment any change reaches, only after being built in Dev and then validated in QA. Testing directly against Production is risky for two concrete reasons: an in-progress or buggy change can lock, corrupt, or simply show wrong numbers in data that live reports depend on right now, and there's no safe way to test something genuinely risky -- a schema change, a large bulk load -- without potentially causing a real outage if it goes wrong. Promoting a change through Dev, then QA, then Production in that fixed order guarantees every change gets at least one chance to fail somewhere that doesn't matter yet before it ever reaches somewhere that does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd frame it around what's allowed to break where. Dev is allowed to break -- that's the whole point of it, it's where I'm actively building and nobody real is looking at it. QA is where I prove a change actually works against data that looks like the real thing, before any real user sees it. Production is the one environment where breaking something has an actual business cost, so it's deliberately the last stop, not the first. If I skipped straight to testing in Production, the two real risks are: a change that's still buggy could corrupt or lock data that a live report is reading from right now, and there's no safe way to rehearse something genuinely risky, like a schema change, without actually risking the outage I was trying to avoid. The fixed Dev-then-QA-then-Production order is really just making sure every change gets tested somewhere low-stakes before it reaches somewhere high-stakes.
commonMistakes: Making a direct change in Production 'just this once' to save time
Treating QA as optional for a change that 'seems small' instead of validating it there first
Letting QA's data drift so far from Production's that it stops catching real issues
Conflating Dev and QA as the same environment instead of recognizing their different purposes (building vs. validating)
keyPoints: Dev is for building and is expected to be unstable, isolated from real users
QA validates a change against production-like data before any real user is exposed to it
Production is the last environment reached, only after Dev and QA
Direct Production changes risk live data and can't safely rehearse risky operations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the purpose of each environment (Dev, QA, Production)
Correctly explains the risk of testing directly in Production
Explains why the promotion order matters

questions.title: Why keep raw data in the bronze layer instead of cleaning it immediately
questions.prompt: In a medallion (bronze/silver/gold) architecture, why deliberately land data into the bronze layer completely raw and unchanged, instead of cleaning and transforming it on the way in to save a step?
questions.modelAnswer: Bronze is a verbatim, untouched copy of exactly what the source sent, kept specifically so there's always a reliable point to reprocess from. If a downstream transformation turns out to have a bug, or a business rule changes months later, having the original raw data still sitting in bronze means reprocessing can start over from the true source again -- if the raw data had been transformed immediately and the original discarded, a bug discovered later could be unrecoverable, because the only copy left is the one built from flawed logic. Silver takes bronze and applies cleaning, deduplication, and conforming to a defined schema; gold aggregates silver into business-ready, consumption-ready tables. Separating these stages also isolates failures: a broken silver transformation doesn't corrupt bronze, and a mistake can be fixed by just rerunning silver against the bronze data that's still safely sitting there untouched.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as an insurance policy, not an extra step for its own sake. Bronze is deliberately a verbatim copy of exactly what the source sent — nothing cleaned, nothing reshaped — specifically so there's always a true, unaltered starting point to go back to. If a bug is found in a silver transformation six months later, or a business rule changes and historical numbers need to be recomputed under the new rule, I can rerun silver against that original bronze data and get it right, because the raw truth never left. If I'd transformed on the way in and thrown away the original, that fix might not even be possible — the only copy I'd have left is the one built from the flawed logic. Keeping the stages separate also means a broken silver job doesn't put bronze at risk at all; I can fix silver and just rerun it.
commonMistakes: Transforming data on ingestion and discarding the raw original, losing the ability to reprocess from the true source later
Treating bronze/silver/gold as just three copies of the same thing
Not reprocessing from bronze after fixing a transformation bug, instead patching only the downstream table and leaving history inconsistent
Skipping the bronze layer entirely to save storage, not realizing what's given up by doing so
keyPoints: Bronze = raw, untouched copy of the source, kept for reprocessing
Silver = cleaned/conformed; gold = business-ready aggregates
Keeping raw data preserves the ability to recover from a downstream bug or a later rule change
Separating stages isolates failures -- a broken silver job doesn't corrupt bronze

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why bronze stays raw/untouched
Correctly describes the roles of silver and gold
Explains the reprocessing/recovery benefit

questions.title: Why land raw data in S3 instead of loading straight into Redshift
questions.prompt: A teammate asks why a pipeline bothers landing raw data in S3 first and only later loading it into Redshift, instead of having the source system write directly into Redshift. What's the architectural reasoning?
questions.modelAnswer: S3 is cheap, durable, and format-agnostic, and landing raw data there first decouples ingestion from any single downstream consumer -- the same raw data in S3 can feed Redshift, be queried directly by Athena, be processed by Glue or EMR, or be reprocessed from scratch if a transformation bug is discovered later, none of which is possible if data is written straight into Redshift with no raw copy preserved anywhere else. Writing directly into a warehouse also couples the source system's write pattern to that warehouse's own ingestion mechanics -- Redshift's COPY command is specifically optimized for bulk loading from S3, not for row-by-row inserts coming from an application -- so staging through S3 first is usually also the mechanically efficient way to get data into Redshift in the first place. This lake-before-warehouse pattern exists precisely to keep the raw source of truth cheap, durable, and reusable by more than one downstream tool, rather than trapped inside one system's storage.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as keeping a cheap, reusable copy of the truth before committing to any one destination. If the source system wrote straight into Redshift, that data is now only reachable through Redshift -- if I later want to run an ad hoc Athena query against it, or reprocess it through Glue because I found a transformation bug, I don't have a raw copy to go back to, I only have whatever Redshift already computed from it. Landing it in S3 first means Redshift, Athena, and Glue can all work from the same raw data independently. There's also a purely mechanical reason I'd bring up: Redshift's COPY command is built to bulk-load efficiently from S3, not to take a stream of individual inserts from an application, so staging through S3 is usually the faster path into Redshift anyway, not just the more flexible one.
commonMistakes: Treating the S3 landing step as pure extra latency instead of recognizing its reuse and recovery value
Not knowing Redshift's COPY command is specifically optimized for bulk loads from S3, not scattered inserts
Discarding the raw S3 copy once Redshift has the data, losing the ability to reprocess or feed other tools later
Coupling the source system directly to one warehouse's availability and schema
keyPoints: S3 is cheap, durable, and decouples ingestion from any single downstream consumer
The same raw S3 data can feed Redshift, Athena, Glue, and EMR independently
Redshift's COPY command is built for bulk loads from S3, not row-by-row application writes
This is the standard lake-before-warehouse pattern for keeping a reusable source of truth

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the decoupling/reusability argument for landing in S3 first
Correctly mentions the COPY-from-S3 mechanical efficiency argument
Clarity of explanation

questions.title: Choosing Athena vs. Redshift for a given workload
questions.prompt: A stakeholder wants to run ad hoc, infrequent queries against a few hundred GB of historical data sitting in S3. Another team runs complex, frequent dashboards against a curated, actively-updated dataset. Which service would you pick for each, and why?
questions.modelAnswer: Athena is serverless and billed per query based on data scanned, with no cluster to provision, size, or pay for when nobody's querying -- which makes it a strong fit for ad hoc, infrequent querying directly against data already sitting in S3, since there's no standing cost and no upfront loading step required. Redshift is a persistent compute resource (provisioned or serverless, but either way always running) better suited to frequent, complex, performance-sensitive queries against a curated dataset, because its columnar storage and distribution/sort keys are specifically built for that repeated, heavier workload -- at the cost of an ongoing bill whether or not it's actively being queried, and generally requiring data to be loaded in first. For the scenario given: the infrequent ad hoc historical queries fit Athena's pay-per-query model well, since there's no reason to pay for standing compute between queries; the frequent, complex dashboard workload fits Redshift's tuned, persistent-compute model better, since repeated heavy queries benefit from its performance optimizations in a way that's worth the ongoing cost.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pick Athena for the first case without much hesitation -- infrequent, ad hoc queries against data that's already sitting in S3 is almost exactly what Athena is built for, and paying only for the data scanned per query beats paying for a Redshift cluster to sit there most of the time doing nothing. For the second team, I'd push toward Redshift -- frequent, complex dashboard queries benefit a lot from distribution keys, sort keys, and result caching that Athena doesn't give you in the same way, and the standing cost of a cluster is actually worth it when it's being used heavily and often. I'd also mention Redshift Spectrum as a bit of a middle ground -- it lets Redshift query S3 directly when needed -- but for a workload this clearly split between 'rare and ad hoc' versus 'frequent and heavy,' I wouldn't overcomplicate it; I'd just pick the tool that matches each team's actual usage pattern.

Picking Athena for a heavy, frequent, complex dashboard workload and getting worse cost/performance than a tuned warehouse
Not knowing Redshift Spectrum lets Redshift also query S3 directly, which can blur the decision in some cases
Ignoring how much data a query actually scans when estimating Athena's real cost
keyPoints: Athena: serverless, pay-per-scan, best for infrequent ad hoc queries directly against S3
Redshift: persistent compute, best for frequent, complex, performance-tuned queries against a curated dataset
Redshift has a standing cost regardless of query frequency; Athena doesn't
Redshift Spectrum bridges the two by letting Redshift query S3 directly when needed

questions.title: Designing a sensible S3 partitioning strategy
questions.prompt: You're landing daily sales data in S3 and know it will mostly be queried by date range and sometimes by region. What partitioning scheme would you use, and what's the basic tradeoff of partitioning too finely versus not partitioning at all?
questions.modelAnswer: A Hive-style partitioning scheme keyed on the most common query filter -- here, something like s3://bucket/sales/year=2026/month=10/day=09/ -- lets query engines like Athena, Glue, or Redshift Spectrum skip entire swaths of data that don't match a query's date filter (partition pruning), dramatically cutting the data scanned and the cost and time of a query. Region could be added as an additional partition level if region-filtered queries are common enough to justify it, but partitioning too finely -- down to the hour, for example, or on a very high-cardinality column -- creates a huge number of small partitions and small underlying files, which has its own cost: it slows down partition-metadata operations and creates the small-file problem, where per-file read overhead starts to dominate over the benefit of pruning. Not partitioning at all sits at the opposite extreme -- every query scans the entire dataset regardless of filters, which gets expensive and slow fast as the dataset grows. The right partition grain balances how the data is actually queried against how many partitions and files that scheme ends up producing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd partition by year/month/day, in that order, since date range is the most common filter here -- that lets a query like 'last 7 days' prune down to almost nothing instead of scanning the whole table. I'd think twice before also partitioning by region underneath that, only adding it if region-filtered queries are actually common enough to be worth the extra partition layer, since every layer multiplies the number of partitions. I'd specifically avoid going down to partitioning by hour just because it's possible -- that's usually a mistake that trades a small pruning benefit for a much bigger small-file problem, since now there are 24 times as many partitions, each potentially holding tiny files. And I'd never leave a dataset like this unpartitioned at all -- every single query would have to scan the whole thing, which gets painfully slow and expensive as more days of data pile up.
commonMistakes: Partitioning by a column that's rarely filtered on instead of the actual common query pattern
Partitioning too finely (e.g., by hour, or a high-cardinality column) and creating a small-file problem
Not partitioning at all, forcing every query to scan the whole dataset
Choosing a partition key order that doesn't match how queries actually filter (outer keys should be the most commonly filtered)
keyPoints: Partition on the columns actually used to filter queries (here, date, possibly region)
Partitioning enables pruning, cutting data scanned and query cost/time
Over-partitioning creates many small partitions/files with their own overhead
No partitioning forces a full scan on every query

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Proposes a sensible partitioning scheme matching the query pattern

questions.title: Event-driven ingestion (Lambda + S3 trigger) vs. a scheduled batch job
questions.prompt: For a pipeline that needs to process each file as soon as it lands in S3, would you reach for an S3 event triggering a Lambda function, or a Glue job running on a fixed schedule? What's the architectural tradeoff?
questions.modelAnswer: An S3 event triggering Lambda processes each file within seconds of it landing, with no polling and no wasted compute between arrivals -- it only runs exactly when there's actually work to do, which fits a workload where low per-file latency matters and each file's processing is small and bounded within Lambda's time and memory limits. A scheduled Glue job running on a fixed interval instead waits for its schedule, picks up everything that's accumulated since the last run, and processes it as a batch -- introducing latency up to the length of that interval, but gaining efficiency when there's genuinely bulk work to do together, and fitting heavier transformations or workloads that exceed what Lambda can handle in a single invocation. The real tradeoff is latency versus workload shape, not which approach is more modern: event-driven Lambda fits frequent, small, time-sensitive units of work; scheduled batch fits heavier, less time-sensitive processing that benefits from being done in bulk.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask two questions before picking: how time-sensitive does this actually need to be, and how big is the per-file work? If the requirement is genuinely 'process it the moment it lands' and each file is small enough to finish well within Lambda's limits, I'd go event-driven -- S3 triggering Lambda directly, no polling, no idle compute between files. If the per-file work is heavier, or a burst of many files landing at once would otherwise spike a lot of concurrent Lambda invocations, I'd lean toward a scheduled Glue job instead, accepting the latency of its schedule interval in exchange for processing everything that's accumulated as one efficient batch. I wouldn't treat this as 'event-driven is always better' -- it's really a question of whether the workload's size and burstiness actually fit inside what a single Lambda invocation handles well.
commonMistakes: Defaulting to event-driven Lambda for a workload that's actually heavy or long-running and hits Lambda's limits
Defaulting to scheduled batch when the business genuinely needs near-real-time processing
Not considering that a burst of many files landing at once can trigger many concurrent Lambda invocations with its own cost/throttling implications
Treating the two approaches as interchangeable regardless of workload size or burstiness
keyPoints: S3-event-triggered Lambda processes files near-immediately, fits small/bounded per-file work
Scheduled batch (Glue) introduces latency up to the schedule interval but suits heavier, bulk processing
The real tradeoff is latency vs. workload shape, not just 'which is more modern'
A burst of many files can trigger many concurrent Lambda invocations, which has its own cost/throttling considerations

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly frames the latency vs. workload-shape tradeoff

Mentions a realistic limitation of each approach

questions.title: Step Functions vs. one Lambda calling the next directly
questions.prompt: A pipeline needs to run three steps in order -- extract, transform, load -- each as its own Lambda function. Why would you put Step Functions in front of them instead of just having each Lambda invoke the next one directly when it finishes?
questions.modelAnswer: Having each Lambda invoke the next directly works for the happy path, but it buries the pipeline's actual structure inside application code spread across three separate functions, with no single place to see the whole flow and no built-in handling for what happens when one step fails -- retries, catching specific errors, and deciding whether to stop or route to a failure path would all have to be hand-written inside each function. Step Functions externalizes that structure into a state machine definition that's visible as a whole, with built-in retry policies and error-catching per state, plus a visual execution history showing exactly which step succeeded, failed, or is still running for any given run. The pipeline's dependency and failure-handling logic ends up living in one declarative place instead of being scattered across each Lambda function's own code -- the same kind of tradeoff as choosing a real orchestrator over chaining scheduled scripts together elsewhere in data engineering.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd put Step Functions in front of this specifically because 'each Lambda calls the next one' hides the pipeline's actual shape inside three separate codebases, and it has no real answer for 'what happens when transform fails halfway through' beyond whatever I happen to hand-code inside that one function. With Step Functions, the whole extract-transform-load flow is visible in one state machine definition, and I get retries and error routing built in per step instead of having to write that logic three separate times. When something breaks at 2 AM, the execution history tells me exactly which of the three steps failed and why, instead of me having to go dig through three different Lambda functions' logs trying to reconstruct what happened. It's the same reasoning as picking a real orchestrator over a chain of scripts calling each other -- it's worth it specifically because there's more than one genuinely dependent step here.
commonMistakes: Hand-chaining Lambdas directly and hard-coding retry/error logic inside each function instead of externalizing it
Having no visibility into which step of a multi-step chain actually failed when something breaks
Coupling each Lambda to knowing about and invoking the next one, making the pipeline harder to change later
Writing custom retry loops inside Lambda code instead of using Step Functions' built-in retry/backoff
keyPoints: Direct Lambda-to-Lambda chaining buries pipeline structure and failure handling inside application code
Step Functions externalizes the flow into a visible state machine with built-in retries and error routing
Step Functions execution history shows exactly which step succeeded/failed for a given run
This mirrors the same tradeoff as choosing a real orchestrator over ad hoc scripting elsewhere

questions.title: Choosing EMR vs. Glue vs. Databricks for a Spark job
questions.prompt: You need to run a Spark transformation job on AWS. What's the basic tradeoff between running it on AWS Glue, on an EMR cluster, or on Databricks on AWS, and what would make you reach for each one?
questions.modelAnswer: Glue is serverless Spark -- no cluster to provision or manage, billed per job run, and tightly integrated with the Glue Data Catalog, which makes it the simplest choice for straightforward, catalog-centric ETL jobs without needing fine-grained cluster control. EMR is a managed but still provisioned Spark cluster, giving far more control over instance types, cluster sizing, and custom configuration, and supporting other big-data frameworks beyond Spark (Hive, Presto, HBase) -- it fits workloads that need that control or scale beyond Glue's simpler model, at the cost of actually managing a cluster's lifecycle, even with EMR automating much of that. Databricks on AWS adds a further layer specifically on top of Spark -- Delta Lake, a polished collaborative notebook environment, and workspace/governance features -- which fits teams that want those specific capabilities and are willing to run on a platform with its own licensing cost on top of the underlying AWS compute. The basic decision axis is how much control or extra capability is needed versus how much operational simplicity is wanted.
questions.professionalAnswer: For a straightforward ETL job that's mostly about reading from the Glue Catalog, transforming, and writing back out, I'd default to Glue -- no cluster to size or babysit, and it's billed per run. If the job needs something Glue's simpler model doesn't give me -- very specific instance types, a non-Spark framework like Hive or Presto, or just more cluster-level control than Glue exposes -- I'd move to EMR, accepting that I'm now responsible for more of the cluster's lifecycle even though EMR automates a lot of it. I'd only reach for Databricks on AWS if the team specifically wants Delta Lake, its notebook environment, or its governance features badly enough to justify its separate licensing cost on top of the AWS compute underneath -- I wouldn't default to it just because it's a popular platform if Glue or EMR would do the job without that extra cost.
commonMistakes: Choosing EMR by default for every Spark job even when Glue's serverless simplicity would do the job with far less operational overhead
Choosing Glue for a workload that genuinely needs cluster-level control or non-Spark big-data tools that EMR supports
Not accounting for Databricks' separate licensing cost on top of the underlying AWS compute
Assuming the three are functionally interchangeable rather than differing in control, integration, and cost model
keyPoints: Glue = serverless Spark, simplest for catalog-centric ETL, least cluster control
EMR = managed but provisioned cluster, more control/scale, supports other big-data frameworks beyond Spark
Databricks on AWS = adds Delta Lake, notebooks, and governance on top of Spark, with its own licensing cost
The decision axis is control/capability needed vs. operational simplicity wanted

questions.title: Redshift Spectrum vs. loading data into Redshift first
questions.prompt: You need to make a large, infrequently-queried historical dataset in S3 available to Redshift users without loading all of it into cluster storage. What feature would you reach for, and why not just load it in with COPY like everything else?
questions.modelAnswer: Redshift Spectrum lets Redshift query data sitting directly in S3, through external tables registered in the Glue Data Catalog, without ever loading it into the cluster's own storage -- which avoids paying for cluster storage and load time for data that's queried rarely and doesn't need the cluster's internal performance optimizations applied to it. Loading everything in with COPY puts the data under full cluster-managed storage and gets the benefit of Redshift's columnar, distribution/sort-key-optimized internal format for the fastest possible repeated queries -- worth the storage and load cost for data that's queried often and needs that performance, but wasteful for a large, infrequently-touched historical dataset that mostly just needs to be occasionally reachable. Spectrum is the right tool specifically when a dataset's query frequency doesn't justify its storage and load cost inside the cluster.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd reach for Redshift Spectrum here rather than COPY, specifically because this data is described as large and infrequently queried -- paying to load all of it into cluster storage, and keeping it there, doesn't make sense for something that mostly just sits there until someone occasionally needs it. Spectrum lets me register it as an external table against the Glue Catalog and query it straight from S3 when needed, without ever committing it to cluster storage. I would flag the tradeoff honestly, though -- Spectrum queries are generally slower than data stored natively in the cluster, since there's no distribution or sort key benefit applied to it, so if usage patterns changed and this dataset started getting queried heavily and needed to be fast, I'd reconsider actually loading it in with COPY at that point.

Using Spectrum for a dataset that's actually queried heavily and would genuinely benefit from being loaded in

questions.title: A basic real-time pipeline with Kinesis Data Streams and Firehose
questions.prompt: A client-facing application generates a continuous stream of clickstream events that need to land in S3 within a few minutes for near-real-time analytics, with minimal custom code to maintain. At a basic architectural level, how would Kinesis Data Streams and Kinesis Data Firehose work together to do this?
questions.modelAnswer: Kinesis Data Streams is the ingestion layer -- the application writes each clickstream event into a stream, which durably retains and orders records across shards and supports multiple independent consumers reading the same stream for different purposes. Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed delivery service that can consume directly from a Data Streams stream and automatically batch, optionally transform (via a Lambda step), and deliver records to a destination like S3, on a configurable buffer interval or size, with no custom consumer code to write or maintain for that delivery path. Putting them together: the application writes to a Data Stream, giving low-latency ingestion plus the option for other consumers -- like a real-time dashboard -- to also read the same events independently, while a Firehose delivery stream subscribed to that same source handles the 'land it in S3 every few minutes' requirement entirely through configuration, rather than a custom consumer application having to be written and operated just to batch and write to S3.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set the application up to write into a Kinesis Data Stream, mainly because that keeps the door open for more than one consumer to read the same raw events later -- a real-time dashboard, for instance, could read from the stream directly while Firehose is also reading from it for delivery. Then I'd attach a Firehose delivery stream to that same Data Stream, configured to buffer and write to S3 every few minutes, which is exactly the 'minimal custom code' part of the requirement -- I'm not writing or running a consumer application myself just to batch records and call S3's API; Firehose does that entirely through configuration. If I knew for certain nothing else would ever need to read these raw events, I'd actually simplify further and have Firehose ingest directly without a Data Stream in front of it at all -- but since the requirement mentions near-real-time analytics, keeping the Data Stream in place for other consumers is the safer architectural call.

Not recognizing Firehose can ingest directly, skipping Data Streams entirely, when no other consumer needs the raw events
Confusing Data Streams (the durable, multi-consumer ingestion layer) with Firehose (the managed delivery mechanism)
Expecting instantaneous delivery from Firehose instead of its buffered interval/size delivery model

The two are often combined when both low-latency multi-consumer access and simple managed S3 delivery are needed

questions.title: What you'd say in your first stand-up
questions.prompt: What is a Daily Scrum (stand-up), and what would you actually say during one in your first week on a new BI team?
questions.modelAnswer: A Daily Scrum, commonly called a stand-up, is a short, time-boxed daily meeting -- often 15 minutes -- where the team synchronizes with itself on progress and blockers; it's explicitly not a status report delivered upward to a manager, it's the team talking to each other. The typical shape each person covers is roughly: what I did since the last stand-up, what I'm doing until the next one, and anything blocking me. A strong first-week answer from a junior team member stays specific and brief rather than vague: naming the actual ticket or task worked on, being honest and specific about being stuck rather than saying a vague 'I'm still working on it,' and flagging a blocker the moment it's identified rather than waiting to mention it, since the whole point of surfacing a blocker in stand-up is getting help from the team quickly, not saving face. A junior new hire should resist the urge to over-explain or justify slow progress at length -- stand-up is meant to be short, and a longer conversation about a specific blocker belongs in a follow-up afterward, not consuming the whole meeting.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd keep it short and specific, something like: 'Yesterday I finished writing the Lookup for the Customer dimension and started on the fact table load. Today I'm wiring up the error output so bad rows get redirected instead of failing the whole package. I'm blocked on getting read access to the QA staging database, so if anyone can help with that after stand-up, I'd appreciate it.' That covers all three parts -- what I did, what I'm doing, what's blocking me -- in under thirty seconds, and it names a real ticket instead of a vague status. I'd also remind myself that stand-up isn't the place to actually solve the blocker; it's the place to surface it so the right person can grab me right after.

questions.title: Recognizing 'blocked' vs. just behind
questions.prompt: You've been working on a ticket and progress has stalled. How do you tell whether you're just behind schedule or genuinely blocked, and how do you communicate that to your team?
questions.modelAnswer: 'Off Track' means the work is simply taking longer than planned -- normal, and usually just needs more time or a closer look, with progress still genuinely possible on your own. 'Blocked' means the work has hit a hard stop entirely outside your control -- a pending approval, a broken test environment, a dependency on another team -- where no amount of your own effort moves it forward until that's resolved. The practical test is asking: is there anything I can still personally do right now to make progress on this? If yes, it's Off Track -- keep working and simply mention in stand-up that it's taking longer than expected. If no -- you're waiting on someone or something outside your control -- it's Blocked, and it should be flagged clearly and immediately, not saved for the next scheduled meeting, since every day a real blocker goes unflagged is a day of work not getting unstuck sooner.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd ask myself one question: is there anything I can actually still do myself, right now, to move this forward? If the honest answer is yes -- I just need more time, or I need to think through the approach again -- that's Off Track, and I'd keep grinding and just flag in stand-up that it's taking longer than I estimated. If the honest answer is no -- I'm waiting on an approval, a broken environment, or someone on another team -- that's genuinely Blocked, and I wouldn't sit on it until the next stand-up. I'd flag it the moment I realize it, specifically naming what I actually need to get unblocked, rather than just saying 'I'm stuck,' because a specific ask is what actually gets someone to act on it quickly.

questions.title: Explaining why the team works in sprints, not all at once
questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks why your team can't just build the whole report and show it to them when it's completely done, instead of working in two-week sprints. How would you explain the difference between Agile and Waterfall to them, and why your team works the way it does?
questions.modelAnswer: Waterfall fits work where the requirements are genuinely stable and fully understood up front, moving through fixed phases once in order -- but if a requirement turns out to be wrong, that's usually not discovered until most of the work is already built, which makes it expensive to fix at that point. Agile instead breaks the same work into short, repeating two-week cycles, each one producing something real and working that the stakeholder can actually see and react to. The explanation should connect directly to the stakeholder's own interest rather than staying abstract: working in sprints means they get to say 'that's not quite what I meant' after two weeks of effort instead of after two months, which protects them, not just the team. It's also worth clarifying that a sprint still produces a genuinely working, shippable piece of the report each cycle -- not an unfinished fragment -- so showing it early isn't showing something broken.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd skip straight to what's in it for them. If we built the whole thing in one long pass and only showed it at the end, and it turned out we misunderstood something on day one, we wouldn't find that out until the entire report was already built -- which is expensive and slow to fix at that point. Working in two-week sprints means every two weeks you get to look at something real and tell us if we're headed the wrong direction, while that's still cheap to correct. I'd also be clear that what you're seeing every two weeks isn't a half-finished mess -- it's a genuinely working slice of the report, just not the whole thing yet. That's really the whole point of sprints: catching a misunderstanding in week two instead of week eight.

questions.title: Communicating during a live production incident
questions.prompt: Two days after a dashboard launches, a regional manager reports it's showing zero sales for their region all month. Walk me through how you'd investigate, and what you would communicate to the manager while you're still figuring out the cause.
questions.modelAnswer: A strong answer separates the two parts of this question clearly. On investigation: start with the simplest explanation before anything complex -- did the dashboard's scheduled refresh actually run last night at all -- then work backward from the visible symptom toward the source, checking whether the ETL load completed for that region, whether the issue is in the underlying data or just a report-level filter, rather than guessing at a cause. On communication: send an honest, specific acknowledgment quickly -- confirming the report was received, that it's being looked into, and giving a concrete time to expect an update -- rather than staying silent until a fix is confirmed. It's expected and professional to communicate while still investigating, not only once the cause is found; silence during that window reads as neglect even when real work is happening behind the scenes.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split this into what I say and what I actually do, and do the communication part first. Within a few minutes I'd send something like: 'Thanks for flagging this -- I'm looking into it now and will have an update for you by end of day.' That costs me almost nothing and tells the manager they haven't been forgotten. Then I'd investigate from the simplest explanation outward: did last night's scheduled refresh actually complete, or did it fail silently? If the refresh ran fine, I'd check whether that region's rows actually loaded into the fact table for this month, or whether this is a filter or slicer issue purely inside the report itself. I'd keep narrowing from the visible symptom back toward the source rather than guessing at something exotic first. Once I actually find the cause, I'd follow up with a clear explanation of what happened and what I changed -- not just a silent fix with no note at all.

Jumping straight to a complex theory instead of checking the simplest thing first (did the scheduled refresh even run)
